forces: Boy soprano solo, orchestra and organ
performers: Denis Thilliez, boy soprano; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: Denis Thilliez, a boy soprano, sings the Requiem’s central prayer, beginning with the organ alone. The melody reaches higher on its second appeal, then settles into the simplest possible plea: two alternating notes.

sections.label: A′ · The second call reaches higher
B · Two notes for everlasting rest
A″ · The first melody returns with winds
sections.mNote: Woodwind solos join the returning soprano melody

sections.label: B′ · The last plea sinks lower
sections.mNote: Two alternating notes, then a rising final requiem

cues.title: A voice above the organ
cues.text: The boy soprano begins in B♭ major, marked dolce e tranquille — sweetly and calmly. Only the organ accompanies him. The orchestra waits through the opening prayer, “Pie Jesu Domine, dona eis requiem”: merciful Lord Jesus, grant them rest.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 61–62: soprano solo, organ and rests in the other instruments. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Boys at the Madeleine
cues.text: At the Madeleine, where Fauré works, women cannot sing in the choir. Boys take the upper parts and the Pie Jesu solo. In the concert hall Fauré prefers women for these lines, with their longer breath and adult voices.
cues.evidence: The Madeleine’s rules and Fauré’s concert-hall preference, citing Jean-Michel Nectoux: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)

cues.title: Two notes for rest
cues.text: “Dona eis” expands the melody, then “sempiternam requiem” — everlasting rest — narrows it to two alternating notes. Muted violas and cellos keep moving beneath the voice. The organ part is marked sempre legato.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 65–66, rehearsals B–C: the expanded phrase, two-note plea and legato organ writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first prayer returns
cues.text: The opening melody returns, now surrounded by soft woodwind solos. Its last plea sinks lower than before. At the end the harp plays quietly, the pace eases, and the voice turns upwards on the final “requiem”.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 67–69, rehearsals D–E: returning melody, woodwind solos, harp and poco rit. at the close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sleeve writer, once a treble
cues.text: Louis Aubert, who signs the sleeve note of this recording, remembers singing the Requiem’s solo soprano part at the Madeleine as a boy of twelve, some months after the first performance. Here the solo belongs to Denis Thilliez, of the Neuilly choir school.
cues.evidence: Louis Aubert’s note on the Erato sleeve (Internet Archive scan): “quelques mois plus tard — j’avais alors 12 ans — … soprano solo de la Maîtrise”; the soloist credit reads “Denis Thilliez, soprano garçon, de la Manécanterie des Petits Chanteurs Notre-Dame de Ste Croix de Neuilly”. https://archive.org/details/faure-o-requiem-cantique-de-jean-racine-louis-fremaux. Wikipedia names Aubert as the treble at the first performance itself: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)

transitions.title: The second prayer reaches higher
transitions.to: A′ · The second call reaches higher
transitions.how: Muted strings, harp and woodwinds answer the first prayer with soft chords. They then withdraw, leaving the soprano and organ to begin again at rehearsal A. The marking is un poco più, and the melody reaches higher than its first statement.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 62–63: orchestral answer and the second call at rehearsal A.

transitions.title: The melody narrows to two notes
transitions.from: A′ · The second call reaches higher
transitions.to: B · Two notes for everlasting rest
transitions.how: The soprano begins “dona eis” softly at rehearsal B over muted lower strings. The organ carries a moving line above its bass notes, marked sempre legato. As the words reach “sempiternam requiem”, the singer settles into two alternating pitches while the accompaniment continues beneath.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 65–66: rehearsals B–C, muted strings, organ and repeated two-note phrases.

transitions.title: The first melody returns with winds
transitions.from: B · Two notes for everlasting rest
transitions.to: A″ · The first melody returns with winds
transitions.how: The two-note plea closes, and “Pie Jesu” begins again on the original melody in B♭ major. Flute, clarinet and bassoon solos join the soprano. The lower strings are marked espressivo, and the bass moves beneath the returning phrase.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 67–68, rehearsal D: B♭ major reprise with woodwind solos.

transitions.title: The last requiem turns upwards
transitions.from: A″ · The first melody returns with winds
transitions.to: B′ · The last plea sinks lower
transitions.how: “Sempiternam requiem” returns in a lower part of the soprano’s voice. The harp plays pianissimo figures over the organ and muted strings. A poco rit. eases the last phrase, which turns upwards before the instruments settle on B♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 69, rehearsal E: lower soprano phrase, harp, poco rit. and final B♭ major chord.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: IV. Pie Jesu, printed pp. 61–69: soprano and organ, muted low strings, harp and woodwind. Flute and clarinet solos accompany the returning melody; the clarinet plays again in the last two bars.

timeline.note: The boy soprano sings with the organ alone. Strings, harp and winds wait.
Woodwind, harp and muted low strings enter pianissimo beneath the voice.
The soprano’s second prayer begins with only the organ beside it.
Soft woodwind, harp and muted strings return before the voice expands its plea.
Muted strings and legato organ accompany “dona eis” and the two-note “sempiternam requiem”.
Flute and clarinet solos join the returning soprano melody; bassoons hold the harmony beneath them.
The voice’s two-note plea sinks lower. Pianissimo harp chords move beneath it.
The first clarinet adds a quiet line in the last two bars. The music slows into the final chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Denis Thilliez (boy soprano), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording. The sleeve credits “Denis Thilliez, soprano garçon” as the only soprano soloist, and the Pie Jesu is the Requiem’s only soprano solo, so his part here is inferred rather than stated. The chorus and baritone have no part in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.88 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 4 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+40 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.37 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: He spent his days at the organ and in the classroom, saving for songs and chamber music the harmonies nobody else could quite imagine.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
The boy kept slipping into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and the little instrument in its chapel gave Gabriel Fauré his first musical happiness. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he lived among plainchant, organ exercises and the interweaving voices of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was done, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers far outside their syllabus. Fauré acquired a teacher, a champion and a friend who would stay beside him for sixty years. He left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine: a French prayer unfolding over a flowing keyboard part, each new choral entry joining a phrase already under way.
